q: Why does `items.forEach(async (x) => { await save(x); })` followed by `console.log('done')` print 'done' before the saves finish, and how do you fix it?

`forEach` ignores the promises returned by its callback, so it returns immediately. Use `for (const x of items) { await save(x); }` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map((x) => save(x)))` to run them concurrently.
`const res = await fetch(url)` succeeds for a URL that returns 404. Is that a bug in fetch?

No. `fetch` rejects only when the request cannot complete (network failure, abort). HTTP error statuses resolve normally with `res.ok === false`, so you must check `res.ok` or `res.status` and throw your own error.
You need results of 3 independent API calls, and the page can still show something if one of them fails. Which combinator fits and why not `Promise.all`?
`Promise.allSettled`: it waits for all three and reports each outcome. `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one call fails, discarding the other results you could have shown.

js-npm-modules.md:
## Why it exists

Nobody writes a web server, a React app or a build script from scratch. JavaScript's strength is its ecosystem: hundreds of thousands of reusable **packages** published to the **npm registry**, plus a standard way to install, version and import them. Two things must be understood to work comfortably with any Node.js, React, Next.js, Vite or TypeScript project: **how dependencies are declared and installed** (npm, `package.json`, the lockfile, semantic versioning) and **how files import each other** (ES modules versus CommonJS). Most "it works on my machine" and "cannot use import statement outside a module" problems live exactly here.

**Mental model:** a project has three layers. `package.json` is the **request** ("I need express, any 4.x"). `package-lock.json` is the **receipt** (the exact versions and checksums that were chosen). `node_modules/` is the **delivery** (the installed files). You commit the first two and never the third; anyone can rebuild the third from the second.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser; **npm** (Node Package Manager) ships with it and talks to the registry. Alternatives with the same model are **pnpm**, **Yarn** and **Bun**; this lesson uses npm. Install an actively supported **LTS** release of Node (see nodejs.org for the current schedule) and, if you work on several projects, a version manager such as nvm, fnm or Volta so each project can pin its own Node version.

The demo uses a folder with three siblings: `app/` (your project) and two tiny local packages, `greeter/` and `legacy-slug/`, that stand in for packages from the registry so every command below works offline. With a real package you would write `npm install express` instead of a folder path.

### Creating a project and package.json

```text
$ mkdir -p app && cd app
$ npm init -y
Wrote to /home/you/demo/app/package.json:

{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC"
}



$ npm pkg set type=module
$ npm pkg set scripts.start="node index.js"
$ cat package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1",
    "start": "node index.js"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC",
  "type": "module"
}
```

Newer npm versions may write slightly different defaults (for example an explicit `"type": "commonjs"`). The fields you will meet most:

```json
{
  "name": "my-service",
  "version": "1.4.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "engines": { "node": ">=22" },
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch src/server.js",
    "test": "node --test",
    "build": "tsc -p .",
    "prepare": "husky"
  },
  "dependencies": { "express": "^4.21.0" },
  "devDependencies": { "typescript": "^5.6.0" },
  "peerDependencies": { "react": ">=18" }
}
```

- **`name` and `version`** identify the package (required to publish). `"private": true` prevents an accidental publish.
- **`type`** decides whether `.js` files are ES modules (`"module"`) or CommonJS (`"commonjs"`, the default).
- **`scripts`** are named commands. `npm run <name>` runs them with `node_modules/.bin` on the PATH, so you can call `tsc` or `vite` without installing them globally. `npm test` and `npm start` are shortcuts. Lifecycle names such as `prepare` and `postinstall` run automatically (see the security note).
- **`dependencies`** are needed at run time; **`devDependencies`** only for development and building (test runners, linters, TypeScript); **`peerDependencies`** are "the host project must provide this" (a React component library declares React this way); **`optionalDependencies`** may fail to install without breaking the install.
- **`engines`** documents the supported Node version (npm only warns unless configured otherwise).

### Installing: npm install, the lockfile and npm ci

```text
$ npm install ../greeter ../legacy-slug --no-audit --no-fund

added 2 packages in 1s
$ cat package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1",
    "start": "node index.js"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC",
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "greeter": "file:../greeter",
    "legacy-slug": "file:../legacy-slug"
  }
}
$ ls node_modules
greeter
legacy-slug
```

`npm install <pkg>` downloads the package and its own dependencies (a tree, sometimes thousands of packages), adds a range to `package.json`, and writes **`package-lock.json`** recording the exact resolved tree. Here the entries say `file:` because the packages are local folders; for registry packages you would see a range such as `"^4.21.0"` and the lockfile would hold the exact version, a download URL and an integrity hash.

- **`npm install`** (no arguments) installs whatever `package.json` allows, updating the lockfile if needed.
- **`npm ci`** ("clean install") deletes `node_modules` and installs *exactly* what the lockfile says, failing if the two disagree. Use it in CI and in Docker builds for reproducible, faster installs.
- Flags you will see: `-D` (save as devDependency), `-g` (global; prefer `npx` or project-local tools instead), `--omit=dev` (production install).

```text
$ rm -rf node_modules
$ npm ci --no-audit --no-fund

added 2 packages in 1s
$ npm ls
app@1.0.0 /home/you/demo/app
├── greeter@1.2.3 -> ./../greeter
└── legacy-slug@1.0.0 -> ./../legacy-slug
```

### Semantic versioning and version ranges

Versions are `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (**semver**): a patch is a bug fix, a minor adds features compatibly, a major may break your code. The range in `package.json` says how far npm may move on its own:

- `^1.2.3` (caret, the default) accepts any compatible change: `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0`. For `0.x` versions the caret is stricter: `^0.2.3` means `>=0.2.3 <0.3.0`, because pre-1.0 minors may break.
- `~1.2.3` (tilde) accepts patches only: `>=1.2.3 <1.3.0`.
- `1.2.3` is exact; `*` or `latest` accept anything (avoid).

```javascript
import semver from "semver";   // npm install semver

console.log(semver.satisfies("1.4.2", "^1.2.3"), semver.satisfies("2.0.0", "^1.2.3"));
console.log(semver.satisfies("1.2.9", "~1.2.3"), semver.satisfies("1.3.0", "~1.2.3"));
console.log(semver.satisfies("0.2.5", "^0.2.3"), semver.satisfies("0.3.0", "^0.2.3"));
console.log(semver.maxSatisfying(["1.2.3", "1.9.0", "2.0.0"], "^1.2.3"));
console.log(semver.satisfies("1.5.0-beta.1", "^1.2.3"));   // pre-releases are excluded from ranges
```

Semver is a promise by the maintainer, not a guarantee; a "minor" release can still break you, which is exactly why the lockfile exists. Inspect and update deliberately: `npm outdated` lists newer versions, `npm update` moves within ranges, `npm install pkg@latest` crosses majors, and `npm ls pkg` shows why a package is installed.

### How Node finds a package: node_modules

When code says `import "greeter"` (a *bare specifier*, not starting with `./` or `/`), Node looks for `./node_modules/greeter`, then `../node_modules/greeter`, and so on up to the filesystem root. Inside the folder it reads that package's `package.json` to learn the entry point: the **`exports`** field (modern, can expose several subpaths and different files for `import` and `require`) or the older **`main`**. Relative imports (`./util.js`) are resolved from the importing file. Package managers *hoist* dependencies, which causes **phantom dependencies**: code can import something it never declared because a sibling package happened to install it, and then it breaks later. Declare everything you import.

{{dg:1}}

### ES modules versus CommonJS

JavaScript has two module systems, a historical accident you must recognise on sight:

- **CommonJS (CJS)**: `const fs = require("fs")` and `module.exports = ...`. Synchronous, the original Node style; also `__dirname` and `__filename`.
- **ES modules (ESM)**: `import fs from "node:fs"` and `export function ...`. The language standard, used by browsers, bundlers and TypeScript source; supports static analysis (tree-shaking) and top-level `await`.

Node decides per file: `.mjs` is always ESM, `.cjs` always CommonJS, and `.js` follows the nearest `package.json` `"type"` (default CommonJS). In ESM there is no `require`, `module` or `__dirname`; use `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+) or `import.meta.url`. Prefix built-ins with `node:` (`node:fs`, `node:path`) so they can never be confused with an npm package. File extensions are mandatory in ESM relative imports (`./util.js`).

The files for the demo (`greeter` is an ES module package, `legacy-slug` is CommonJS):

```json
// file: greeter/package.json
{ "name": "greeter", "version": "1.2.3", "type": "module", "exports": { ".": "./index.js" } }
```

```javascript
// file: greeter/index.js
export function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
```

```json
// file: legacy-slug/package.json
{ "name": "legacy-slug", "version": "1.0.0", "main": "index.js" }
```

```javascript
// file: legacy-slug/index.js
module.exports = function slug(text) {
  return text.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-|-$/g, "");
};
```

```javascript
// file: app/index.js
import { greet } from "greeter";
import slug from "legacy-slug";

console.log(greet("World"), slug("Node Modules 101"));
```

```text
$ npm start

> app@1.0.0 start
> node index.js

Hello, World! node-modules-101
$ npm run
Lifecycle scripts included in app@1.0.0:
  test
    echo "Error: no test specified" && exit 1
  start
    node index.js
```

Mixing the two: **ESM can import CommonJS** (the `module.exports` value becomes the default import, as above). **CommonJS can `require()` an ES module** in recent Node versions (22.12 and newer, as long as the module has no top-level `await`); older versions threw `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` and forced `await import()`. A dynamic `import()` works everywhere and returns a promise.

```javascript
// file: app/interop.mjs
import { greet } from "greeter";
import slug from "legacy-slug";                 // CommonJS: module.exports is the default import
import { sep } from "node:path";

console.log(greet("Ada"), slug("Hello, Module World!"));
console.log(typeof require, typeof module, import.meta.filename.endsWith("interop.mjs"));
const { default: legacy } = await import("legacy-slug");   // dynamic import + top-level await
console.log(legacy === slug, sep);
```

```javascript
// file: app/old.cjs
const slug = require("legacy-slug");
const { greet } = require("greeter");   // require() of an ES module (Node 22.12+)
console.log(slug("CommonJS Still Works"), greet("Grace"));
console.log(typeof __dirname, require.main === module);
```

```text
$ node interop.mjs
Hello, Ada! hello-module-world
undefined undefined true
true /
$ node old.cjs 2>&1
commonjs-still-works Hello, Grace!
string true
```

### TypeScript, bundlers and dev servers

Browsers cannot read TypeScript, JSX or bare imports like `import "react"`. A **bundler** (Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup, Turbopack, Parcel) compiles your source, resolves every import through `node_modules`, removes unused code (tree-shaking), minifies, splits it into chunks and fingerprints the filenames for caching. **Vite** is the common default for new front-end projects: its dev server serves your modules on demand (fast start, instant hot updates) and `vite build` produces the optimised production bundle. Frameworks such as Next.js, Remix and Nuxt wrap a bundler plus routing and server rendering.

```sh
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev      # development server with hot reload
npm run build    # optimised output in dist/
npm run preview  # serve the production build locally
```

Recent Node versions can also run TypeScript files directly by *stripping* type annotations, with no compile step (only syntax that can simply be erased; `enum` and similar need extra flags). It does **not** check types, so keep `tsc --noEmit` in your checks.

```javascript
// file: app/hello.ts
type User = { name: string; age: number };
const u: User = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
console.log(`${u.name} is ${u.age}`);
```

```text
$ node hello.ts
Ada is 36
```

## Worked example

You inherit a project and must get it running, safely:

1. `git clone` it and read `package.json`: check `engines`, `scripts`, and whether a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `yarn.lock`) exists. The lockfile tells you which package manager to use; never mix two.
2. Switch to the right Node version (`nvm use`, `fnm use` or Volta reads `.nvmrc` or the `engines` field).
3. `npm ci` (not `npm install`) to get exactly the recorded tree. If it fails because the lockfile is out of sync, that is a bug to fix in the repository, not to paper over.
4. `npm run` lists the scripts; start with `npm test`, then `npm run dev`.
5. To add a library: `npm install zod`, read its README, check its maintenance and size, and commit both `package.json` and the updated lockfile in the same commit.
6. When a build says `Cannot find module 'x'`, ask: is it declared (`npm ls x`)? Is it a relative path missing its extension in ESM? Is `type` right? When it says `require is not defined in ES module scope` or `Cannot use import statement outside a module`, the file's module type and its syntax disagree: rename to `.cjs` or `.mjs`, or fix `"type"`.

## In real products

- **CI pipelines** run `npm ci`, then lint, test and build; they cache the npm download cache (not `node_modules`) keyed on the lockfile hash.
- **Dockerfiles** copy `package.json` and the lockfile first, run `npm ci --omit=dev`, then copy the source, so the dependency layer is cached until the lockfile changes.
- **Monorepos** use workspaces (npm, pnpm, Yarn) to hold several packages in one repository that depend on each other without publishing; tools like Turborepo and Nx cache builds across them.
- **Library authors** publish both ESM and CommonJS builds through `exports`, with TypeScript declaration files, so every consumer works.
- **Dependency bots** (Dependabot, Renovate) open pull requests for updates so versions move steadily and with review instead of in a once-a-year panic.

> [!pitfall] Committing `node_modules/` or editing files inside it. Add it to `.gitignore`; changes there vanish at the next install. Patch packages with a documented patch tool or a fork.

> [!pitfall] Running `npm install` in CI or deployment instead of `npm ci`, and ignoring lockfile diffs in code review. A changed lockfile is a changed supply chain; look at what moved.

> [!pitfall] Using `*`, `latest` or very wide ranges, or importing a package you did not declare (a phantom dependency). Both turn a routine reinstall into a surprise breakage.

> [!pitfall] Forgetting file extensions and `"type"` in ESM, or using `__dirname` in an ES module. Use `import.meta.dirname` and write `./util.js`, not `./util`.

> [!tip] Prefer `npx` or project scripts over global installs, pin the Node version in `.nvmrc` or `engines`, run `npm ls <pkg>` to find out why something is installed, and use `npm pack --dry-run` to see what a package would publish.

> [!tip] Before adding a dependency ask: could the platform do this (`fetch`, `node:test`, `URL`, `structuredClone`)? How big is it, when was it last released, how many maintainers does it have? Every dependency is code you run and a person you trust.

> [!cost] A single innocent `npm install` can pull in hundreds of transitive packages, slow installs, large Docker layers and bigger front-end bundles (and bundle size is paid by every visitor on every phone). Audit with `npm ls --all`, bundle analyzers and `npm install --omit=dev` in production images.

> [!security] The npm ecosystem is a prime supply-chain target: typosquatted names, hijacked maintainer accounts, malicious updates and **install scripts** (`preinstall`, `postinstall`, `prepare`) that run arbitrary code on your machine at install time. Mitigate with committed lockfiles and `npm ci`, reviewing new or suddenly changed dependencies, `npm install --ignore-scripts` for untrusted code, `npm audit` (useful but incomplete), scoped private packages with a registry configured to prevent dependency confusion, and two-factor authentication plus provenance or trusted publishing for packages you publish. Never put secrets in `package.json` or `.npmrc` files that are committed.

> [!prod] Production checklist: lockfile committed and enforced with `npm ci`; Node version pinned and matching CI and Docker; `NODE_ENV=production` with dev dependencies omitted; automated update PRs; an SBOM or dependency scan in CI; a private registry mirror or cache for resilience; and an `engines` field plus a CI matrix across the Node versions you support.

> [!version] Verified 2026-10-21 in the sandbox on Node 22.22.2 with npm 10.9.7, offline: every transcript was generated by running the commands against local folder packages (timings in the npm output were normalised to `1s`), the `file:` dependency and lockfile behaviour, `npm ci`, `npm ls`, ESM importing CommonJS, `require()` of an ES module, `import.meta.filename` and `node hello.ts` (TypeScript type stripping worked without a flag here) were all observed, and the semver examples were run against npm's bundled copy of the `semver` package. NOT verified: any download from the real registry, Vite commands (no network), newer npm versions' `npm init` defaults, the behaviour of `require()` of ESM or type stripping on other Node versions (the version numbers 22.12 and 20.11 come from the Node documentation as I know it, not from a run), pnpm, Yarn and Bun specifics, and the security mitigations and publishing features (provenance, trusted publishing), which are described from general knowledge and change often.
q: When should CI use npm ci instead of npm install?
Almost always: it installs exactly what package-lock.json records, deletes node_modules first and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree, so builds are reproducible.
What does ^0.2.3 allow, and why is it different from ^1.2.3?
For 0.x versions the caret allows only patch updates (>=0.2.3 <0.3.0) because minor bumps before 1.0 may break compatibility; ^1.2.3 allows up to <2.0.0.
A file fails with 'require is not defined in ES module scope'. What is wrong?
The file is an ES module (.mjs or type: module) but uses CommonJS. Use import (or createRequire), rename it to .cjs, and use import.meta.dirname instead of __dirname.

dg.cap: Types exist only at check time. The JavaScript that runs has none, so untrusted data must be validated at runtime.
Use both: schemas guard the boundary, types keep the interior consistent.
n: Runtime validation at the edge (Zod, Valibot)

q: Why do type annotations not protect you from a malformed API response?
They are erased at compile time. At runtime the JSON is whatever the server sent; you need runtime validation (e.g. a Zod schema) to prove its shape.
What is structural typing and what problem does branding solve?
Types are compatible when shapes match, regardless of names. So two string IDs are interchangeable; a brand (string & { __brand }) makes UserId and OrderId distinct at compile time.
What does the 'never' check in the default branch of a switch give you?
Exhaustiveness: if a new union variant is added and not handled, the assignment to never fails to compile, pointing you to every switch that needs updating.
How does unknown differ from any?
any disables checking and spreads; unknown forces you to narrow or validate before using the value.
What does satisfies do that a type annotation does not?
It validates a value against a type without widening it, so you keep the precise literal types for inference.
Why must CI run a separate type-check step even though the bundler compiles TypeScript?
Bundlers like SWC and esbuild only strip types; they do not check them. tsc --noEmit (or tsgo) is what actually reports type errors.
